payload.snippet: You accidentally kick your ball through your neighbour's window.
options: Tell your parent and go apologise straight away
Run inside and pretend it wasn't you
Blame someone else
Wait to see if they notice
payload.explanation: Owning up to accidents quickly is always the right thing to do.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour asks you not to play loud music near their window while their baby sleeps.
options: Move further away or play more quietly
Turn the music up louder
Argue that you were there first
Play music anyway because it's your garden
payload.explanation: Being considerate of others' needs, especially babies sleeping, is good neighbourly behaviour.

payload.snippet: The man next door slips on ice at the bottom of his steps.
options: Ask if he is hurt and tell your parent
Laugh and go inside
Walk past without saying anything
Tell him he should have been more careful
payload.explanation: Checking if someone is hurt and getting a grown-up is the caring and sensible thing to do.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour leaves a note asking you to keep the shared path clear of bikes.
options: Move your bike and say thank you for letting you know
Leave the bikes where they are
Take down the note and ignore it
Write a rude reply
payload.explanation: Respecting shared spaces and being gracious about polite requests keeps neighbours happy.

payload.snippet: You notice the lights in the house next door have been on all night and no one has opened the curtains.
options: Mention it to a parent or trusted adult
Ring the doorbell every hour
Break a window to check inside
Ignore it completely
payload.explanation: Mentioning an unusual observation to a trusted adult is the safe and sensible action.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour grows prize roses and you accidentally break one off playing in the garden.
options: Tell your parent and offer to apologise to the neighbour
Push the broken flower back into the soil
Throw it away and say nothing
Blame the wind
payload.explanation: Honesty and offering an apology shows responsibility and earns respect.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour brings home-baked biscuits to your door as a thank-you for helping them.
options: Say thank you warmly and share them with your family
Say you don't want them and close the door
Take them without saying anything
Give them back and say you don't eat biscuits
payload.explanation: Accepting a kind gift graciously and saying thank you makes the other person feel appreciated.

payload.snippet: A parcel is delivered to your house that is addressed to your neighbour.
options: Bring the parcel next door as soon as possible
Open it to see what's inside
Leave it outside in the rain
Keep it and say nothing
payload.explanation: Returning a wrongly delivered parcel quickly is honest and considerate.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour is away on holiday and their wheelie bin is blocking the shared path.
options: Move the bin to the side so people can pass
Leave it blocking the path — not your problem
Tip the bin over
Go through their garden to move it further away
payload.explanation: Helping with a small inconvenience when a neighbour is away is a kind community gesture.

payload.snippet: You see two children from the street throwing stones at your neighbour's fence.
options: Tell a trusted adult what you saw
Join in
Shout at them yourself
Say nothing because they might bully you
payload.explanation: Telling a trusted adult about property damage is the right action — it's not telling tales, it's being responsible.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's child falls off their bike right in front of you.
options: Check if they are hurt and help them up
Keep cycling past
Laugh and ride away
Go home and tell your parents later
payload.explanation: Stopping to help someone who has fallen is a basic act of kindness.

payload.snippet: The photo came out very dark.
options: Move to a brighter spot
Close the curtains
Take fewer photos
Put the camera away
payload.explanation: Photos taken in dark places are hard to see. More light makes them much better.

payload.snippet: The picture is all blurry.
options: Hold the camera very still and try again
Shake the camera more
Put a filter on
Make the photo smaller
payload.explanation: Blurry photos happen when the camera moves. Keeping still helps the camera capture a sharp image.

payload.snippet: Your finger is covering part of the lens.
options: Move your finger away from the lens
Keep your finger there
Take the photo anyway
Add a sticker over it
payload.explanation: Covering the lens blocks the view. Always check your fingers are clear before pressing the button.

payload.snippet: The sun is shining right into the camera lens.
options: Turn so the sun is behind you
Close your eyes and press the button
Take the photo straight into the sun
Put sunglasses on the camera
payload.explanation: Shooting into the sun makes photos very bright and hard to see. Keeping the sun behind you gives a much clearer picture.

payload.snippet: The dog keeps moving every time you press the button.
options: Wait until the dog is sitting still
Make the dog run faster
Take a photo of something else
Put the dog in a box
payload.explanation: Moving subjects come out blurry. Waiting for a still moment helps you get a sharp, clear photo.

payload.snippet: The photo shows the inside of your pocket.
options: Take the phone out properly and try again
Keep taking photos in your pocket
Use the front camera
Delete all photos
payload.explanation: Accidental pocket photos happen when the camera button is pressed by mistake. Taking the phone out first solves it.

payload.snippet: You want to take a photo of a rainbow but it is very far away.
options: Zoom in to make the rainbow look bigger
Run towards the rainbow
Only photograph the sky
Wait for another rainbow
payload.explanation: Zooming brings distant things closer in the frame so you can see them better in the photo.

payload.snippet: Your photo has a big shadow across it.
options: Move so your shadow does not fall on the subject
Make the shadow bigger
Add more shadows on purpose
Turn off the lights
payload.explanation: Shadows in photos can block the subject. Moving your position so the shadow falls elsewhere fixes it.

payload.snippet: The colours in the photo look orange and strange indoors.
options: Turn on more lights or open the curtains
Take the photo in the dark
Use only one light
Paint the room a different colour
payload.explanation: Indoor lights can make photos look orange. More daylight or brighter lights help colours look natural.

payload.snippet: You want a photo of your whole family but there is no one to press the button.
options: Use the timer setting so the camera takes the photo automatically
Leave one person out
Hold the camera very far away
Draw a photo instead
payload.explanation: The timer lets you set the camera down, get in position, and have the camera take the photo on its own.

payload.snippet: The photo has too many people's heads cut off at the top.
options: Step back further so everyone fits in the frame
Make the people shorter
Only photograph feet
Tilt the camera upside down
payload.explanation: Stepping back gives more room in the frame so everyone's head and body can fit into the picture.

payload.snippet: It is night time and everything looks black in the photo.
options: Turn on a light near the subject
Take photos only at night
Close your eyes to take the photo
Use the photo as a bookmark
payload.explanation: Cameras need light to capture an image. A nearby light source brightens the subject so it shows up clearly.

payload.snippet: You want a photo of a butterfly but it flies away before you can press the button.
options: Wait very quietly and still for the butterfly to land again
Chase the butterfly waving your arms
Take a photo of a flower instead
Give up and go inside
payload.explanation: Patience is important in nature photography. Staying quiet and still gives wild creatures time to settle.

payload.snippet: The photo has a big pole growing out of someone's head.
options: Move to a different angle where the pole is not behind the person
Cut the photo in half
Saw the pole down
Ignore it
payload.explanation: Distracting objects in the background can be removed simply by changing your position slightly.

payload.snippet: You take a photo of your drawing but the paper looks very white and bright.
options: Move to indirect light instead of direct sunshine
Draw on darker paper
Hold the drawing behind a curtain
Only photograph in the dark
payload.explanation: Direct sunlight bleaches out white paper. Soft indirect light preserves the colours and details of your drawing.

payload.snippet: Your selfie only shows the top of your head.
options: Hold the camera a little higher and tilt it down slightly
Take a photo of just your hair
Ask a friend to take it instead
Stand on a chair
payload.explanation: Holding the camera slightly above eye level and tilting it down creates a flattering angle that shows your whole face.

payload.snippet: The photo is too small to see the details of your model you built.
options: Move the camera closer to fill the frame with the model
Build a bigger model
Put the model far away
Use a smaller camera
payload.explanation: Getting closer to a subject fills the frame with detail, making it much easier to see in the finished photo.

payload.snippet: You want to photograph the moon but it looks like a tiny white dot.
options: Use as much zoom as possible and keep the camera very still
Throw the camera up in the air
Wait until the moon is bigger
Turn off the zoom
payload.explanation: The moon is very far away; maximum zoom combined with a very steady hold gets the best detail.

payload.snippet: Your birthday photo has red glowing eyes.
options: Turn off the flash and use a lamp nearby instead
Give everyone red-eye drops
Use a bigger flash
Add red sunglasses to the photo
payload.explanation: Red eye is caused by flash reflecting off the retina. Using ambient light instead of direct flash eliminates the effect.

payload.snippet: The background of the photo is very messy and distracting.
options: Move the subject to a cleaner spot or step closer to fill the frame
Add more mess to make it fair
Take the photo from below
Edit the background orange
payload.explanation: A clean or simple background keeps the viewer's attention on the subject rather than the clutter behind them.

payload.snippet: You are doing a puzzle and cannot find the last piece.
options: Look under the table and cushions where it might have fallen
Give up and throw the puzzle away
Colour in a piece of paper to replace it
Blame your brother
payload.explanation: Puzzle pieces often fall under furniture. Checking nearby surfaces and the floor is always worth a try.

payload.snippet: Two puzzle pieces look exactly the same but one does not fit.
options: Try both and use the one that clicks in smoothly
Force the wrong one in with your fist
Cut the piece to make it fit
Throw both away
payload.explanation: Similar-looking pieces are common in puzzles. Gently trying each one and feeling for the click tells you which is correct.

payload.snippet: You accidentally sit on one puzzle piece and it bends.
options: Gently flatten it under a heavy book
Throw it away immediately
Keep it bent so you know which one it is
Hide it at the back of the box
payload.explanation: A bent piece can often be flattened by placing something heavy on it for a few minutes.

payload.snippet: The puzzle box has a picture but the pieces are all face down.
options: Turn all the pieces face up before you start
Build the puzzle with the pieces face down
Put all the brown pieces together
Give up because you cannot see the picture
payload.explanation: Turning all pieces face up first gives you the whole picture to work with and makes it much easier to match shapes and colours.

payload.snippet: You are halfway done but need to go for dinner.
options: Leave the puzzle on the table and come back after dinner
Sweep it all back into the box
Take the puzzle to the dinner table
Ask your mum to finish it
payload.explanation: Leaving the puzzle where it is means you can carry on where you left off without losing your progress.

payload.snippet: You cannot tell which side is the right way up for one puzzle piece.
options: Compare it to the picture on the box to find the right orientation
Try all four ways until one looks right
Glue it in anyway
Skip that piece
payload.explanation: The box picture is your guide — comparing the colours and patterns on the piece to the picture quickly shows which way it should go.

payload.snippet: The puzzle is too big for the table.
options: Move to the floor where there is more space
Build only half the puzzle
Cut the board in half
Fold the puzzle up
payload.explanation: Large puzzles need lots of space. The floor gives you plenty of room to spread out and see all the pieces.

payload.snippet: A small child has chewed one puzzle piece and now it does not fit properly.
options: Contact the puzzle maker to ask for a replacement piece
Try forcing it in
Leave a gap in the puzzle
Put the chewed piece at the edge where gaps show less
payload.explanation: Many puzzle companies will send replacement pieces if you contact them. In the meantime, leaving the gap is better than forcing a damaged piece.

payload.snippet: You pick up a piece that looks like it should go in a gap but the colour is slightly wrong.
options: Set it aside and try other pieces first
Colour it in with a marker to match
Jam it in since it almost fits
Tear the hole bigger so it fits
payload.explanation: If a piece almost fits but the colour is off, it belongs somewhere else. Keeping it separate and coming back to it often finds the right spot.

payload.snippet: You have sorted all the edge pieces but now cannot find a corner.
options: Check for pieces that have two flat sides — those are the corners
Start in the middle instead
Assume there are no corners in this puzzle
Empty the box and start again
payload.explanation: Corner pieces are the only ones with two straight sides at a right angle. Looking specifically for that shape finds them quickly.

payload.snippet: The puzzle is of a blue sky and every piece looks the same blue.
options: Sort by the exact shade of blue and look at the shapes
Give up because all sky puzzles are impossible
Use only the edge pieces
Glue all the blue pieces together randomly
payload.explanation: Even a uniform sky has slight tonal and colour variations. Sorting by subtle shade differences, then matching the irregular shapes, is the key to tricky sky sections.

payload.snippet: You drop the puzzle from the table and all the pieces scatter.
options: Collect all the pieces and start sorting them again
Cry and refuse to start over
Glue whatever lands together
Decide the puzzle is done
payload.explanation: Accidents happen. Patiently collecting and re-sorting gives you a fresh start and you will often find pieces you missed before.

payload.snippet: One puzzle piece fits but leaves a visible white gap around its edges.
options: Remove it and keep looking — a slightly different piece will fill the gap completely
Accept the gap as part of the design
Fill the gap with white paint
Declare the puzzle finished anyway
payload.explanation: A visible gap means the piece is almost but not quite right. The correct piece will fit snugly with no gap showing.

payload.snippet: You want to do a puzzle but all the pieces are still in the bag from the shop.
options: Empty all the pieces onto the table first, then turn them face up
Try to build the puzzle with pieces still in the bag
Pour the pieces back into the box and use the box lid as a tray
Only take pieces out one at a time as you need them
payload.explanation: Emptying all pieces and turning them face up before starting gives you the full picture to work from and is much more efficient.

payload.snippet: Your puzzle picture shows a garden and you do not know where to start.
options: Find and build the straight-edged border first
Pick any piece from the middle and work outward
Sort by which pieces you like best
Only do the flower parts first
payload.explanation: Building the frame first gives you a defined shape and boundary that makes filling in the middle much easier.

payload.snippet: Two friends both want to do the same puzzle at the same time.
options: Agree to each work on a different section of the puzzle
Only one person does the puzzle and the other watches
Divide all the pieces into two equal piles
Race to see who can place pieces fastest
payload.explanation: Dividing the puzzle into sections lets both friends work simultaneously, making it go faster and keeping everyone involved.

payload.snippet: You have finished the puzzle but one piece is missing even after searching everywhere.
options: Accept the puzzle is complete except for one piece and display it anyway
Tear the whole puzzle up in frustration
Fill the gap with chewing gum
Accuse someone of stealing the piece
payload.explanation: One missing piece from a finished puzzle is a common experience. The work is still complete and worth celebrating. You can always look for the piece again later.

payload.snippet: Your dog has stolen a puzzle piece and is chewing it in the corner.
options: Calmly swap the piece for a treat so the dog releases it
Chase the dog around the room
Shout at the dog until it drops the piece
Let the dog keep it and order a new puzzle
payload.explanation: A calm treat swap is the most effective way to retrieve something from a dog's mouth without a chase game developing.

payload.snippet: The puzzle has 1000 pieces and looks very hard.
options: Sort pieces into colours and patterns before placing any
Try to do it all in one sitting without sorting
Only do 100-piece puzzles
Sort only the red pieces and ignore the rest
payload.explanation: Sorting a large puzzle into colour groups first makes the actual assembly much less overwhelming and more systematic.

payload.snippet: You realise you have put a section of the puzzle in the wrong place.
options: Carefully remove the wrong section and reposition it correctly
Leave it and hope no one notices
Rip up the wrong section
Cover the error with a sticker
payload.explanation: Fixing errors as soon as you notice them is easier and less frustrating than discovering mistakes at the end when the misalignment becomes impossible to ignore.

payload.snippet: The magician asks for a volunteer from the audience.
options: Raise your hand if you want to go up on stage
Run onto the stage without being asked
Shout until the magician picks you
Hide under your seat
payload.explanation: Raising your hand politely is the right way to let the magician know you want to volunteer.

payload.snippet: The magician pulls a rabbit out of an empty hat.
options: Clap and cheer for the trick
Grab the rabbit
Tell everyone how it was done
Run up and look in the hat
payload.explanation: Enjoying the magic and showing appreciation with applause makes the show fun for everyone.

payload.snippet: The magician makes a coin disappear and asks where it went.
options: Say you do not know and enjoy the mystery
Accuse the magician of stealing
Look inside the magician's sleeve
Demand the coin back
payload.explanation: Part of the fun of magic is not knowing how tricks work. Enjoying the mystery is what makes magic special.

payload.snippet: The magician does a trick but you do not understand what happened.
options: Wait and watch carefully for the next trick
Ask the magician to explain every trick
Leave the show
Tell the magician the show is confusing
payload.explanation: Magic is meant to be surprising and mysterious. Watching carefully is more fun than asking for explanations.

payload.snippet: The audience is too loud and the magician cannot be heard.
options: Be quiet and listen so everyone can enjoy the show
Talk even louder
Tell the audience to be quiet by shouting
Leave the show
payload.explanation: Being a good audience member by staying quiet helps everyone around you enjoy the performance.

payload.snippet: The magician asks the audience not to tell how a trick is done.
options: Keep the secret so others can enjoy the surprise
Tell all your friends the secret
Write the secret in your diary
Pretend you did not hear
payload.explanation: Keeping magic secrets means other people get to enjoy the same surprise you did.

payload.snippet: The magician drops a card by accident during a card trick.
options: Wait quietly and let the magician carry on
Pick up the card and look at it
Laugh and point
Tell everyone the trick is ruined
payload.explanation: Performers sometimes make small mistakes. Being patient and kind gives them the chance to continue the show.

payload.snippet: The magician asks you to pick a card and remember it.
options: Look at the card, remember it, and put it back when asked
Show everyone your card immediately
Pick two cards
Forget which card you chose on purpose
payload.explanation: Following the magician's instructions carefully helps the trick work correctly for everyone.

payload.snippet: A dove flies out of the magician's cape and into the audience.
options: Stay still and let the magician's assistant collect the bird
Chase the dove around the room
Try to catch the bird yourself
Shout and wave your arms
payload.explanation: Staying calm keeps the bird safe. Chasing it would scare the animal and ruin the show.

payload.snippet: The magician makes flowers appear from thin air.
options: Clap and admire the flowers
Grab the flowers from the magician
Ask where the flowers were hidden
Say the flowers are fake
payload.explanation: Appreciating the moment is part of enjoying a magic performance. Clapping shows the magician you liked the trick.

payload.snippet: The magician tells a long story before the main trick.
options: Listen carefully because the story is part of the magic
Talk to your friend while waiting
Ask the magician to skip to the trick
Walk out to get a snack
payload.explanation: In magic performances, the storytelling builds suspense and is part of the act — it makes the trick feel more impressive.

payload.snippet: You are sitting at the back and cannot see the small object the magician is holding.
options: Lean slightly to the side to improve your view without blocking others
Stand on your chair
Push past people to get to the front
Call out asking the magician to hold it higher
payload.explanation: Leaning slightly is considerate; standing on chairs or pushing past others disrupts everyone around you.

payload.snippet: The magician invites children to come forward for a group trick.
options: Walk calmly forward if you want to join in
Run forward and push to the front
Refuse because you are shy but shout from your seat
Pull a friend forward who does not want to go
payload.explanation: Walking calmly shows respect for others. Never force someone to take part if they do not want to.

payload.snippet: The magic show ends and the magician takes a bow.
options: Stand up and clap to show your appreciation
Walk out immediately without clapping
Ask for another trick right now
Tell the magician which tricks you did not like
payload.explanation: Applauding at the end of a performance is a way of saying thank you to the performer for their hard work.

payload.snippet: The magician asks if anyone has a wand for the next trick.
options: Raise your hand if you have something to offer
Run onto the stage and grab the magician's own wand
Say you have a wand even if you do not
Ignore the question
payload.explanation: Honest participation helps the trick work. Raising your hand politely is the correct way to volunteer an object.

payload.snippet: The magician makes something disappear and asks where it went.
options: Guess along with everyone else and enjoy the surprise of the reveal
Shout out the answer if you know how the trick works
Refuse to guess because you do not know
Stand up to get a better look behind the screen
payload.explanation: Guessing along and enjoying the reveal is part of the audience experience. Spoiling the trick for others by revealing the method is unkind.

payload.snippet: During the show a young child near you starts crying because they are scared of the magician's mask.
options: Quietly reassure the child that it is just a costume and not real
Tell the child to stop crying because it is just a show
Ignore the child and keep watching
Call out to the magician to take the mask off
payload.explanation: A gentle, quiet reassurance helps the child without disrupting the performance or making them feel embarrassed.

payload.snippet: The magician calls your name as the volunteer for the big finale.
options: Walk up with a smile and follow the magician's instructions carefully
Refuse to go up even though you volunteered
Go up but do things your own way to make it more interesting
Ask the magician to pick someone else
payload.explanation: Volunteering and then following instructions makes the trick work properly. The magician has rehearsed it carefully.

payload.snippet: The magician shows that both hands are empty before producing a flower.
options: Accept that the mystery is the point and enjoy the moment
Accuse the magician of hiding it in the sleeve when the hands looked empty
Grab the flower to check if it is real
Close your eyes so you do not see the trick
payload.explanation: The excitement of magic is that the moment seems impossible. Accepting the mystery is the spirit of the experience.

payload.snippet: The magician asks the audience to shout a magic word together.
options: Join in enthusiastically with the rest of the audience
Stay silent so you do not look silly
Shout a different word to confuse the magician
Cover your ears
payload.explanation: Participating with the audience together is part of the fun and helps create the shared magic experience.

payload.snippet: The train door opens at your stop.
options: Wait for people to get off before you get on
Push onto the train right away
Hold the door open with your foot
Stay on the platform
payload.explanation: Letting people off first makes it easier and safer for everyone to board and exit the train.

payload.snippet: You cannot find your ticket on the train.
options: Look carefully through all your pockets
Jump off at the next stop
Pretend you have a ticket
Ask the conductor to let you off
payload.explanation: Checking all your pockets carefully often finds a lost ticket. Staying calm helps you think clearly.

payload.snippet: The seat next to you has someone's bag on it.
options: Politely ask if you can sit there
Sit on the bag
Move the bag onto the floor without asking
Stand the whole journey
payload.explanation: Politely asking is the respectful way to request a seat. The owner can move their bag.

payload.snippet: The train is very crowded and you cannot find a seat.
options: Stand in a clear area and hold a rail
Sit on the floor in the middle of the aisle
Ask someone to give you their seat immediately
Block the doors so you can leave quickly
payload.explanation: Standing safely with a rail to hold is the correct way to travel when seats are full.

payload.snippet: Your snack is making a loud crunching noise on the quiet train.
options: Save the noisy snack for a less quiet moment
Eat as fast as possible
Offer snacks to every passenger
Put the snack in your bag
payload.explanation: Being considerate of other passengers means avoiding noisy eating on quiet trains.

payload.snippet: The train stops in a tunnel and the lights flicker.
options: Stay seated and wait calmly
Pull the emergency handle
Try to open the train door
Start shouting for help
payload.explanation: Trains sometimes pause briefly in tunnels. Staying calm and seated is the safe thing to do until normal service resumes.

payload.snippet: A very old man is standing near you on the busy train.
options: Offer him your seat
Pretend not to see him
Ask the conductor to find him a seat
Move to a different carriage
payload.explanation: Offering a seat to an elderly person who is standing is a kind and considerate thing to do.

payload.snippet: You need to go to the bathroom but do not know where it is.
options: Ask the train conductor politely where the toilet is
Go between the carriages
Wait until the end of the journey
Ask random passengers loudly
payload.explanation: The conductor knows the train and can direct you quickly. Asking politely is the right approach.

payload.snippet: Your phone starts playing music loudly in the quiet carriage.
options: Turn the volume off immediately
Keep it playing because it is a good song
Plug in headphones quickly
Move to the next carriage still playing music
payload.explanation: Turning off noise immediately is more respectful than trying to fix it by other means. Other passengers deserve quiet.

payload.snippet: You drop litter on the train floor by accident.
options: Pick it up and put it in the bin or your bag
Leave it because you did not mean to drop it
Kick it under the seat
Wait to see if someone notices
payload.explanation: Picking up accidental litter is the right thing to do. Trains should be kept clean for all passengers.

payload.snippet: A baby is crying loudly in your train carriage.
options: Be patient and understanding — babies cannot help crying
Complain to the parent loudly
Move to another carriage if it bothers you
Tell the baby to be quiet
payload.explanation: Babies cry and parents cannot always stop it. Being patient and kind is the right attitude. Moving carriages is fine if you prefer, but complaining is not helpful.

payload.snippet: You leave your bag on the overhead rack and get off the train before remembering.
options: Tell a station worker immediately so they can contact the train crew
Run back to the platform but the train has already left
Call the train company from outside the station
Wait at the station and hope the bag is returned
payload.explanation: Reporting a left item immediately gives the best chance of recovery before the train reaches the next station.

payload.snippet: The train is arriving at your stop but the doors have not opened yet.
options: Wait for the doors to open by themselves
Repeatedly press the door button before the train stops
Try to pull the door open manually
Jump off from the window
payload.explanation: Train doors open at the correct time. Pressing buttons before the train stops or pulling manually is unsafe.

payload.snippet: A stranger on the train asks you where you are going.
options: Give a vague answer or say you are with a grown-up nearby
Tell them your exact destination and home address
Ignore them completely without saying anything
Ask them where they are going instead
payload.explanation: It is sensible not to share personal details with strangers. A polite, vague reply is fine and does not put you at risk.

payload.snippet: The conductor asks to see your ticket but it is on your phone with low battery.
options: Show the ticket as fast as you can before the battery dies
Ask the conductor to wait while you find a charger
Tell the conductor the ticket is saved in your email
Pretend to show the screen while covering part of it
payload.explanation: Acting quickly while you still have battery is the best approach. Inspectors understand briefly if you explain calmly.

payload.snippet: You hear a loud bang from somewhere on the train.
options: Stay seated and wait for an announcement from the train crew
Pull the emergency stop handle immediately
Open the carriage door and look outside
Tell every passenger to evacuate
payload.explanation: Unexpected sounds are usually minor technical issues. Waiting for official guidance from the crew is the safe and correct response.

payload.snippet: Your train is delayed and you will be late for your sports match.
options: Text your coach to let them know about the delay
Jump off at the next stop and run the rest of the way
Ask the conductor to speed the train up
Give up and go home
payload.explanation: Letting your coach know in advance is polite and gives them time to make arrangements. Delays are sometimes unavoidable.

payload.snippet: A child on the train is drawing on the seat with a felt tip pen.
options: Gently tell them that drawing on seats is not allowed
Take the pen away immediately
Tell the conductor straight away
Ignore it because it is not your problem
payload.explanation: Politely telling a child is the kindest first step. It gives them the chance to stop before involving an adult.

payload.snippet: You feel sick on the train.
options: Tell your adult companion and ask to sit near the doors for fresh air
Get off at the next stop by yourself
Lie down on the seats
Hold on until you reach your destination
payload.explanation: Telling an adult immediately gets you help. Sitting near doors where air circulates often helps with travel sickness.

payload.snippet: The train journey is very long and you are bored.
options: Read a book, listen to music with headphones, or look at the scenery
Walk up and down the aisles repeatedly
Talk loudly on the phone the whole journey
Ask the conductor for entertainment
payload.explanation: Quiet entertainment like reading or headphones keeps you occupied without disturbing other passengers.

payload.snippet: The sandcastle fell over.
options: rebuild it
cry
swim
leave
payload.explanation: Building sandcastles teaches persistence.

payload.snippet: A wave splashed her feet.
options: jump back
run away
sit down
scream
payload.explanation: Waves at the shore surprise you suddenly.

payload.snippet: He found a shiny shell.
options: pick it up
throw it
bury it
ignore it

payload.explanation: Offering to help fixes the cause for both of you.

payload.snippet: The man across the road parks across your driveway every weekend, and your dad is stuck because his shift starts in twenty minutes and he can't get out.
options: knock on his door politely and ask him to move now
leave a furious note tucked under his windscreen wiper
block his car in next weekend to teach him a lesson
phone the police because dad is going to be late for work
payload.explanation: A polite knock now is faster than a note or police call.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's cat keeps using your mum's vegetable patch as a toilet, and your dog ate something from the soil last week and was very unwell afterwards.
options: ask the neighbour and add cat-deterrent plants around the bed
throw the cat over the fence whenever you see her there
feed the cat treats so she stops hunting in your garden
stop growing vegetables because of one neighbour's cat
payload.explanation: Honest chat plus deterrent plants protects the dog and the friendship.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's house alarm has been going off all morning and they're away on holiday for two weeks, and the noise is giving your gran a terrible headache.
options: check if they left an emergency contact and ring that person
phone the police because the noise is upsetting your gran
climb their fence to see if you can switch it off
ignore it because the alarm will run out of battery eventually
payload.explanation: Emergency contacts exist for exactly this kind of holiday alarm.

payload.snippet: The neighbour with three small dogs lets them out at five every morning to bark in the garden, and your dad has finally lost patience after a month of it.
options: encourage dad to talk to her in the day before he loses it
go round at five tomorrow morning to film the dogs barking
complain to the council about the morning noise straight away
buy the dogs treats so they like you and bark less
payload.explanation: Daytime calm chats land better than five-am confrontations.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's tree has grown right over your back garden and now half the lawn never gets sun, and your mum says the grass is dying off in patches.
options: ask the neighbour if you can trim the branches over your side
chop the branches off without asking and clear up later
let the lawn die and lay artificial grass instead
report the tree to the council as overgrowth
payload.explanation: Asking first respects the tree and the neighbourly relationship.

payload.snippet: You see your neighbour's nine-year-old climbing out of her bedroom window onto the porch roof, and you're not sure if she's playing or trying to run away.
options: call up to her gently and tell her parents about it
shout at her to get down before she falls off
video it on your phone in case she falls afterwards
wait to see what happens before getting involved
payload.explanation: Telling her parents now prevents either play or running away ending badly.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour brought you a homemade pie because you helped with her shopping, but you're vegetarian and the pie is full of beef and onion gravy.
options: thank her warmly and quietly give the pie to your dad
tell her you're vegetarian so she remembers next time
throw the pie out and never mention it to her
eat the pie anyway so you don't hurt her feelings
payload.explanation: A warm thanks now and a gentle mention next time both work.

payload.snippet: Your elderly neighbour confides that her son hasn't visited her for two years and she's lonely, but she made you promise not to mention it to your mum.
options: encourage her to ring her son and check in on her regularly
keep the secret and forget she ever mentioned it
tell mum anyway because it's too sad to keep quiet
ring the son yourself from her phone without asking
payload.explanation: Encouraging her own call respects her wishes and her loneliness.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour put up a tall fence right along the path you both share, and now your bins won't fit through the gap to reach the front for collection.
options: show her the bin problem and ask for a small adjustment
push the fence over because it shouldn't be there
carry bins through the house every collection day forever
report her fence to planning permission straight away
payload.explanation: Showing the bin problem makes the issue obvious and fixable.

payload.snippet: The new family next door has a teenage daughter who keeps blasting music from her car at half past seven every morning before she leaves for college.
options: leave a friendly note explaining your baby brother sleeps through that time
smash her wing mirror so she's late and doesn't bother again
blast your own music back at her each evening loudly
post a warning on the street's WhatsApp group anonymously
payload.explanation: Notes about the actual reason are far easier to act on.

payload.snippet: Your next-door neighbour's son just got his first car and you can smell strong petrol fumes coming from their open garage every evening this week.
options: tell your parents so they can pop round and ask about it
ring the fire brigade about a possible petrol leak nearby
open all your windows to clear the smell from your house
wait a week and see if the smell goes away on its own
payload.explanation: Parents popping round is faster and less alarming than fire engines.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour offers to mind your puppy while you're at football, but her own dog is aggressive and your puppy is still too young to defend himself properly.
options: thank her and explain you'd rather book a proper dog sitter
agree because she's the friendly neighbour and it's free
agree but ask her to keep the dogs in separate rooms
say yes once and never let her dogsit again afterwards
payload.explanation: Honest declines keep your puppy safe and the friendship intact.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour asks to borrow your dad's drill for ten minutes, but last time she borrowed his ladder she kept it for two months before returning it.
options: lend it but agree on a return time before she takes it
lend it without saying anything and hope she returns it
refuse to lend it because of the ladder problem before
lend her a different drill so dad's stays at home safe
payload.explanation: Agreed return times prevent the same problem happening again.

payload.snippet: You spotted your neighbour's young child wandering the street alone in pyjamas at half past seven on a Sunday morning while everyone else was still asleep.
options: walk her home and knock loudly until a parent answers
leave her be because she clearly came out by herself
video her so you have proof for the parents later
take her into your house and wait for someone to notice
payload.explanation: Knocking until a parent answers reunites her safely and quickly.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's car alarm goes off every time a heavy lorry rumbles past your road, and tonight it's already woken your gran up three times after midnight.
options: ring the neighbour now because they probably can't hear it
bang on their door until they come out to disable it
throw a stone at the car to set off the alarm fully
complain to the council in writing on Monday morning
payload.explanation: A phone call lets them switch it off before the next lorry.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour invites your family to a barbecue but you know they're struggling with money, and your mum says they shouldn't be feeding the whole street.
options: go but bring a homemade salad and dessert to share
go empty-handed because they invited you not the other way
make an excuse so they save money by not feeding you
go but only eat a tiny bit so they have leftovers
payload.explanation: Bringing food turns the barbecue into a proper shared meal.

payload.snippet: You took a candid photo of your friend laughing during lunch and it's really sweet, but she's got food round her mouth and would hate it being shared.
options: show her first and only post it if she gives the okay
post it because it captures a genuine happy moment
share it just to your close-friends story so it's smaller
send it to her in private and tease her about her face
payload.explanation: Showing first respects her face and keeps the friendship safe.

payload.snippet: Your photography club project is due Monday and the best landscape shot you took has another kid's little brother in the corner without his parents' permission.
options: crop the brother out and submit the landscape clean
submit it because it's mostly landscape anyway
blur his face and hope nobody notices the change
ask the kid if he minds and skip his parents
payload.explanation: Cropping protects the child and keeps the landscape strong.

payload.snippet: Your dad asks you to take a family Christmas photo on his proper camera, but you've never used it and he's already pouring everyone a drink in the lounge.
options: ask him for a two-minute tutorial before everyone gathers
take the photo on auto and hope it comes out fine
use your phone instead and email it to him afterwards
say no and ask a relative who knows the camera
payload.explanation: A two-minute tutorial saves a blurred family Christmas memory.

payload.snippet: Your friend wants you to take photos of her in her new gymnastics leotard for her social media, but she's twelve and her dad keeps her account private for safety.
options: say yes only if her dad sees the photos before posting
take the photos because they're just for her account
take them but say she shouldn't post them publicly
refuse to take any photos of her in the leotard at all
payload.explanation: Dad's preview is the safety system that's already in place.

payload.snippet: You sneak a photo of your teacher tripping over a bin during assembly and the whole class wants you to AirDrop it round the year group right now.
options: delete it because it would humiliate her in front of everyone
share it because it's just a funny harmless moment
share it only to your three closest friends quietly
keep it on your phone but promise not to share it
payload.explanation: Adult humiliation spreads fast — delete now, not later.

payload.snippet: Your gran asks you to scan old family photos but one of the boxes contains pictures of relatives who've passed away, and your mum gets emotional seeing them suddenly.
options: scan a few and show mum gently before going through them all
scan them all in one go to get the job done
skip the box and tell gran you couldn't find it
show mum every single photo as you scan them in
payload.explanation: A gentle preview lets mum brace before the harder photos.

payload.snippet: Your friend posts a photo you took of you both at the beach, but she's cropped you out of the picture and only kept herself looking great in it.
options: ask her kindly to credit you as the photographer in the caption
unfollow her and tell other friends what she did
comment publicly that you took the photo so everyone sees
stop taking photos of her ever again from now on
payload.explanation: A kind ask gives her a chance to fix it without drama.

payload.snippet: You're taking photos at your cousin's wedding rehearsal as a favour and your aunt asks if you can also film the speeches with one hand while shooting.
options: say honestly that you can't do both well and suggest one job
agree because she's family and you don't want to upset her
agree but warn the footage and photos might be poor
do it but skip taking photos during the speeches
payload.explanation: Honest limits beat ruined photos and ruined speech footage.

payload.snippet: Your phone storage is full from class trip photos and the museum gift shop has internet, but downloading from cloud will use up your monthly mobile data limit.
options: use the museum's free wifi to back up and free space
delete photos at random until your phone has space
carry on without backing up and hope nothing breaks
switch to mobile data even though it'll cost your parents
payload.explanation: Free wifi in shops is exactly what travel days are for.

payload.snippet: Your school newspaper wants a photo of the football team but the captain is off sick on the only day everyone else is free for the shoot.
options: ask the team if you can reshoot when she's back
take the photo without her and crop her into it later
use last season's photo even though three players have left
leave the team off the newspaper page this issue
payload.explanation: Reshooting honours the captain and gets a real team photo.

payload.snippet: You snapped a great shot of your dog mid-jump but your finger covered the lens slightly, leaving a black smudge on one side of the photo you can't edit out.
options: accept the smudge and use it as a learning lesson on grip
lie and say the smudge is artistic vignetting on purpose
delete it because no good photo has a smudge in it
ask your sister to edit it with a paid app on her phone
payload.explanation: Learning lessons from real mistakes makes you a better photographer.

payload.snippet: Your friend wants you to photograph her birthday party but her parents have a strict rule that no children's faces can be posted online without their families' permission.
options: take photos but agree they stay on the family camera roll only
take them and let the parents sort out permissions later
take backs-of-heads photos so nobody's face is shown
refuse to take any photos because of the parent rules
payload.explanation: Camera-roll-only respects the rule and still captures memories.

payload.snippet: Your gran's eightieth birthday photo album is your responsibility but you accidentally left the camera on the bus on the way home, and the lost property line is closed.
options: phone the bus depot first thing tomorrow and tell gran honestly
pretend you didn't take any photos at the party
blame your little brother for distracting you on the bus
buy gran a new camera to make up for losing hers
payload.explanation: Honest now plus the depot call gives the album its best chance.

payload.snippet: Your photography teacher wants the class to shoot strangers on the high street for an urban portrait project, but you feel uncomfortable photographing people without asking first.
options: tell her your concern and ask if you can shoot with consent
do it because the teacher said so and grades matter most
shoot people from behind so they don't see their faces
skip the project entirely and accept the low grade
payload.explanation: Telling her opens a conversation that might help the whole class.

payload.snippet: Your friend asks you to delete a group photo because she doesn't like how she looks, but you and four others love the photo and want to keep it as a memory.
options: delete it for her but ask the others to keep their copies
keep posting it because the majority wins in the group
delete it from everywhere and tell the others tough luck
edit her out and post the picture without her in it
payload.explanation: She controls her image; others control their copies separately.

payload.snippet: Your camera's battery dies just before your nephew's first steps and your phone is charging in the kitchen plug downstairs, two flights away.
options: film with your eyes and write the moment down straight after
sprint downstairs and hope he repeats the steps for you
borrow your sister's phone without asking permission first
miss the moment and don't bother writing anything down
payload.explanation: Some moments live in stories better than in shaky later video.

payload.snippet: You spotted a brilliant sunset but the best view is from a neighbour's front lawn, and you'd need to step over their low fence to get the right angle for the shot.
options: knock on the door and ask politely for one quick photo
climb the fence quickly because they're probably not home
shoot from the pavement and zoom in as best you can
wait until tomorrow when the sunset might be just as good
payload.explanation: Knocking respects the lawn and often gets a friendly yes.

payload.snippet: Your friend's photography post on Instagram is actually your shot that you sent her last week, and she's tagged it with her own credit and got hundreds of likes.
options: message her privately and ask her to credit you instead
comment publicly that the photo is stolen from you
report the post to Instagram and let them deal with it
let it go because likes don't really matter anyway
payload.explanation: Private messages give friends a chance to fix things kindly.

payload.snippet: Your class trip is to a temple where photography is forbidden inside, but your friend keeps sneaking shots and posting them to the group chat as you walk round.
options: ask her to stop and explain it disrespects the place
report her to the teacher straight away with proof
ask for the photos because they look really good actually
pretend you didn't notice and don't say anything to her
payload.explanation: A quiet ask first respects both her and the temple's rules.

payload.snippet: You're shooting your sister's school play and the school says no flash because it distracts the actors, but the lighting is so low your photos are coming out completely blurry.
options: lift your phone steady on a railing and shoot without flash
use flash just once for the curtain call at the end
switch to your phone's automatic mode and ignore the rule
give up and watch the play without taking any photos
payload.explanation: Steady against a railing handles low light without breaking rules.

payload.snippet: Your friend gave you a 2000-piece jigsaw for your birthday but ten pieces are missing from the box, and her mum already wrote a lovely message inside the lid.
options: tell your friend gently so her mum can swap it with the shop
complete what you can and pretend the puzzle was perfect
throw the whole jigsaw away without saying anything
buy the same puzzle yourself to replace the missing pieces
payload.explanation: Gentle honesty lets her mum sort the shop and keeps trust.

payload.snippet: Your form team is doing a school escape room and your friend always rushes ahead solving every clue alone, so the rest of you never get a chance to think.
options: ask her quietly to let others try the next clue first
complain loudly so the whole team hears how unfair it is
let her carry on and don't bother trying any clues yourself
race her to the next clue so she doesn't get there first
payload.explanation: A quiet ask keeps the team game from becoming her solo run.

payload.snippet: You're stuck on a Sudoku for the school maths puzzle prize and your friend offers to text you the answer she got from her older sister yesterday afternoon.
options: say no thanks and keep trying it yourself slowly
take the answer because the prize is really good
take the answer but pretend you worked it out yourself
report your friend to the teacher for offering to cheat
payload.explanation: The prize for solving is the solving, not the prize itself.

payload.snippet: Your gran loves crosswords but the print in her usual paper is now too small for her glasses, and she's been giving up on them for weeks without saying why.
options: buy her a large-print crossword book for her birthday
tell her she should just get stronger reading glasses
do the crosswords for her and read out the answers
stop giving her crossword books for any future birthday
payload.explanation: Large-print books fix the actual problem without changing her glasses.

payload.snippet: Your little brother is doing a puzzle that's too hard for him and starts crying because he can't finish, but you have homework due in tomorrow morning.
options: do twenty minutes with him then go back to your homework
finish the whole puzzle for him so he stops crying
tell him to do an easier puzzle and walk away
tell mum he's crying and let her deal with it
payload.explanation: Twenty minutes shared usually unsticks him without losing homework time.

payload.snippet: Your friend is convinced the answer to the riddle is 'fire' and won't listen to anyone else, but you're pretty sure it's 'breath' from a similar one you saw online.
options: share your answer and let the group decide together
agree with her so she doesn't get upset at you
tell her she's wrong and stop being so stubborn
look up the answer online and quietly check first
payload.explanation: Group puzzles work when everyone's idea actually gets aired.

payload.snippet: Your class quiz team has one round left and you're three points behind, but your strongest subject is the next round and your friend wants to swap captain to her.
options: stay calm, play to your strengths, and stick with the captain
swap captain because she's been wanting to lead all term
argue loudly about the captain in front of the other teams
give up early because you probably can't catch up anyway
payload.explanation: Captain swaps mid-quiz rarely help and often confuse the team.

payload.snippet: You finished a 1000-piece puzzle with your gran over a week and she wants to glue it for the wall, but the table is also used for family dinners and homework.
options: suggest moving it to a board first then gluing it there
glue it on the table and eat dinner around it for now
take it apart and start a new one together instead
put it away in the box and forget about gluing it
payload.explanation: Moving to a board saves both the puzzle and the dinner table.

payload.snippet: Your puzzle club leader gave you a free Rubik's cube but you found a YouTube guide that solves it in twenty seconds, and your friend wants you to teach her the trick.
options: teach her the steps but encourage solving without watching
refuse because she should figure it out by herself first
teach her and tell her the trick is the actual skill
do it for her every time so she never has to learn
payload.explanation: Knowing the steps still leaves the real solving to her hands.

payload.snippet: Your form room has a daily puzzle on the whiteboard and your friend rubs out the answer before anyone else can try, because she finishes first every morning.
options: ask the teacher for the puzzle copy you can both keep covered
start coming in earlier than her to beat her to the board
rub her answer out and write your own answer up there
stop trying the puzzle because she ruins it every day
payload.explanation: A covered copy means everyone gets the puzzle, not just the early bird.

payload.snippet: Your sister's birthday escape room booking has space for six and one friend dropped out last minute, but if you go in five the puzzles become much harder.
options: ring two cousins now to see if either can join in time
go with five and complain about the harder puzzles after
cancel the whole booking and lose the deposit money
go with four because someone else might cancel too
payload.explanation: Two cousins is a quick call that protects the booking and her party.

payload.snippet: Your gran's old jigsaw is missing one corner piece and she's stuck on it for months, but you saw an identical jigsaw at the charity shop for two pounds today.
options: buy the charity-shop one and slip the corner piece into hers
tell her the puzzle is unfinishable and to give up
buy the new one and let her start the puzzle again
leave it and hope the corner piece turns up later
payload.explanation: Two pounds finishes her months of work in one quiet swap.

payload.snippet: Your friend cheats at the school chess puzzle club by moving her pieces when you look away, and now she's on the leaderboard above other kids who actually played fair.
options: talk to her honestly and offer to play without distractions
copy her cheating so you both end up on the leaderboard
tell the chess club leader without warning her first
stop going to chess club because she's ruining it for you
payload.explanation: An honest chat gives her a chance before involving the leader.

payload.snippet: Your maths puzzle homework is due in the morning and you've been stuck on the last question for hours, while your friend already sent the answer to the group chat.
options: look at the method, hide the answer, and try the method yourself
copy the answer because everyone else in the chat will
send the same wrong answer as your friend to be safe
leave the question blank and explain to the teacher
payload.explanation: The method teaches; the answer alone doesn't.

payload.snippet: Your puzzle book is full of stickers your little cousin put on every page, and you wanted to do the dot-to-dots that are now hidden under the stickers completely.
options: peel the stickers off gently and explain stickers are for sticker pages
throw the book away because it's totally ruined now
tell your cousin off so she never touches your things again
do the puzzles on top of the stickers and ignore them
payload.explanation: Gentle peeling plus a calm explanation saves both the book and her feelings.

payload.snippet: You're building a giant Lego puzzle with your dad but he keeps rebuilding the bits you've finished his way, and you're starting to feel like you might as well stop helping.
options: tell him kindly that you'd like to finish your own sections
stop building and let him do the whole thing alone
rebuild his sections your way to see how he likes it
build it perfectly so he can't find anything to fix
payload.explanation: Telling him kindly is fairer than quitting or copying his behaviour.

payload.snippet: Your school treasure-hunt puzzle leads to a tree in the headteacher's private garden, and the clue says to dig at the base to find the next envelope hidden there.
options: ask the headteacher's permission before digging in her garden
dig quickly while she's at lunch and replace the soil neatly
skip the clue and try to guess the final answer without it
tell the teachers their hunt has a bad clue and stop playing
payload.explanation: Permission turns a risky dig into a fun moment with the head.

payload.snippet: Your team's puzzle solution at scout camp is correct but you got it because a different team accidentally shouted theirs across the field at the same time.
options: tell the leader honestly so they can decide what counts
claim the answer because you heard it fair and square
say nothing and hope nobody noticed the shout either
tell the other team they helped you so they get credit too
payload.explanation: Leader's call is the only fair way to handle accidental overhearing.

payload.snippet: Your friend's puzzle game on her tablet has loot boxes that cost real money, and she's been asking her mum's card details to buy the next batch of hint coins.
options: tell her honestly that loot boxes are designed to trap her spending
help her ask her mum so she doesn't have to do it alone
buy a few coins yourself and give them to her as a gift
stop playing her game so you don't have to see it anymore
payload.explanation: Honest words about loot box design help her see it for herself.

payload.snippet: Your family puzzle night was meant to be tonight but your sister has a maths puzzle test tomorrow and is panicking, asking if you can swap puzzle night for next week.
options: swap to next week and help her revise puzzles tonight instead
refuse the swap because puzzle night was planned first
do both — puzzle night and revision at the same table
swap nights but skip helping her revise to keep some fun
payload.explanation: Swapping plus helping turns her test stress into a team night anyway.

payload.snippet: You're doing a magic show at your sister's birthday party and the card trick goes wrong because the wrong card flips out for everyone to see clearly.
options: laugh, own the mistake, and offer to try one more trick
claim you meant to do that and bow proudly anyway
blame the deck and storm off in front of the kids
pretend you didn't see the wrong card flip out
payload.explanation: Owning the mistake keeps the audience on your side.

payload.snippet: Your friend wants to copy the rope trick you learned from your magic kit but she keeps showing the audience the secret during her rehearsal in the playground.
options: show her the hand position that hides the secret first
let her perform it badly so people stop asking her
tell her she's not allowed to copy your tricks at all
video the secret moment and send it to her group chat
payload.explanation: Helping the hand position protects the trick for both of you.

payload.snippet: The school talent show audience includes a kid who saw your coin trick last week and is loudly shouting how it works to everyone around him.
options: smile, swap to a different trick you haven't shown him
argue with him from the stage in front of everyone
do the trick anyway and hope nobody is listening
stop the show and demand he be moved to the back
payload.explanation: A backup trick saves the show without an argument.

payload.snippet: Your magic kit's vanishing scarf trick is missing the special pocket and your cousin's birthday party where you promised to perform is in three hours.
options: swap it for a simpler trick you can do well today
perform it anyway and hope nobody notices the missing pocket
cancel the whole magic show with no warning
buy a new kit from the shop on the way to the party
payload.explanation: A simpler trick done well beats a complicated one fumbled.

payload.snippet: Your friend laughs during your magic show because she saw the trick at her birthday party last month, and now the other kids are starting to lose interest.
options: ask her to be your assistant on the next bigger trick
tell her to leave the room until the show is over
skip ahead to your finale to win them back fast
carry on quietly and ignore the kids who lost interest
payload.explanation: Turning her into the assistant makes the loss of secrecy a win.

payload.snippet: Your little brother breaks your favourite magic prop trying to figure out the trick and lies to your face when you ask what happened to it.
options: show him you know calmly and ask him to help fix it
shout at him until he admits what he broke
go straight to mum and demand he replace your prop
break one of his toys so he learns how it feels
payload.explanation: Calm honesty teaches him better than shouting or revenge.

payload.snippet: You want to do a fire-based magic trick like the magicians on TV, but you're eleven and your parents are at work and your gran is downstairs napping.
options: wait until parents are home and ask them to supervise
try it once quickly in the bathroom over the sink
do it outside in the garden where it's safer
use a candle from the dining room since it's smaller
payload.explanation: Fire tricks need awake adults, full stop.

payload.snippet: Your magic show is meant to last fifteen minutes but you've burned through all your tricks in seven minutes, and parents at the back are checking watches now.
options: do encore versions of your best trick with new volunteers
end the show early and apologise to all the parents
make up a new trick on the spot without practice
ask the audience to give you ten more minutes to plan
payload.explanation: Encore versions stretch time without inventing anything you can't do.

payload.snippet: Your friend wants to be your magician's assistant for the school fete but she's nervous and keeps forgetting her cues during every single rehearsal you do.
options: give her smaller cues with hand signals to make it easier
replace her with someone who actually remembers the cues
do the show alone and not have an assistant after all
shout her cues from the stage so she remembers them
payload.explanation: Smaller hand-signal cues work for nervous assistants on the day.

payload.snippet: The card you palmed has stuck to your sweaty hand and won't drop properly during the reveal, and the audience is staring expectantly while you try to recover.
options: pause, joke about magic being hot work, and try once more
dump all the cards on the floor and walk away from the table
force the card down and reveal the wrong one anyway
blame the audience for sitting too close to the table
payload.explanation: Honest jokes give you a moment to recover the trick.

payload.snippet: Your magic teacher told the class never to reveal tricks, but your little sister keeps crying because she's scared of the disappearing rabbit she just saw at your show.
options: show her the secret quietly so she stops being scared
tell her magic is real and the rabbit is in another world
tell her not to come to your magic shows anymore ever
tell teacher about her crying and ask what to do
payload.explanation: Family fear breaks the rule kindly — secrets aren't worth tears.

payload.snippet: Your show needs a deck of cards but you only have a chess set and three pencils, and your local shop is closed because it's a Sunday afternoon.
options: build a show around mind-reading tricks with the pencils
cancel the show because you don't have any proper cards
use the chess pieces as cards and confuse everyone
borrow cards from a neighbour without asking permission first
payload.explanation: Pencil mind-reading is real magic that needs no cards.

payload.snippet: Your big trick involves a volunteer from the audience but the only kid who volunteered is your friend who already knows exactly how the trick works.
options: thank her and ask for a second volunteer to actually use
use her anyway and hope she pretends to be surprised
skip the trick and do a different one without volunteers
tell the audience there are no volunteers and stop early
payload.explanation: A real surprised volunteer keeps the trick honest and fun.

payload.snippet: Your magic mentor at after-school club catches you using a trick deck for a class show that's meant to be honest tricks only, and other kids notice the deck.
options: own up, swap to honest tricks, and apologise to your class
pretend the trick deck is a normal deck and bluff it out
blame your mentor for not warning you clearly enough
leave the magic club early so you don't get told off
payload.explanation: Owning up and swapping tricks repairs trust with class and mentor.

payload.snippet: Your friend's birthday magic show has to be quiet because her newborn baby brother is asleep, but your best trick involves an audible drumroll and a big shout.
options: swap the drumroll for a finger-snap and a whisper reveal
do it loudly and apologise to her mum if he wakes up
skip the trick because it needs the noise to work
ask her to wake the baby first so noise doesn't matter
payload.explanation: Quiet versions of tricks work and keep babies asleep.

payload.snippet: Your magic show is for ten-year-olds but one of the parents is heckling and trying to expose every trick, ruining the experience for the kids watching.
options: kindly thank her and ask her to enjoy from the back
argue with her in front of all the kids she upset
ignore her and just shout louder than her over the tricks
cancel the show and refuse to perform until she leaves
payload.explanation: Kind redirection protects the kids without ruining the parent's day.

payload.snippet: Your magic prop arrives broken in the post and the show is tomorrow, with no time for a replacement to arrive and your savings already spent on the original.
options: email the seller for a refund and use simpler home tricks
use the broken prop and hope it holds together on stage
cancel the show and disappoint everyone who was coming
ask the seller for an urgent next-day replacement free
payload.explanation: Refund plus home tricks saves the show and the savings.

payload.snippet: You're performing at your gran's care home and one of the residents is shouting out wrong guesses loudly during every trick, distracting all the other watching residents.
options: include her warmly and turn her guesses into part of the show
ask the staff to take her out so others can enjoy
tell her to be quiet so the show can finish properly
skip your remaining tricks and end the show early today
payload.explanation: Including her warmly turns disruption into delight for everyone.

payload.snippet: The magic kit you got for Christmas has a trick where you 'eat' a balloon, but you can't get the secret right and you're choking slightly each time you practise.
options: stop practising the trick and ask online forums for help
keep practising because you'll get the hang of it soon
do the trick at the show without practising enough
swallow the balloon for real to make the trick easier
payload.explanation: Tricks that choke you need expert help before practice continues.

payload.snippet: Your magic show at the fete made twenty pounds for charity, but you also kept five pounds for sweets without telling the school council it came from the takings.
options: give the five back to the council and apologise honestly
keep the money because you did all the work yourself
tell the council you spent it on more magic props instead
give it back without saying why and hope they don't ask
payload.explanation: Honest return restores trust and keeps the charity total true.

payload.snippet: Your gran's train ticket is digital but her phone has died on the platform, and the inspector is already walking down the carriage checking everyone's tickets.
options: show your ticket and explain about gran's dead phone politely
pretend gran isn't with you so she's not asked at all
argue with the inspector that the rules are unfair
hide gran in the toilet until the inspector has moved on
payload.explanation: Polite explanations to inspectors usually get a sensible solution.

payload.snippet: You spot an empty four-seater on a busy commuter train but it has bags on every seat, and the woman in the next row says they're hers and she's holding them.
options: ask politely if she'd mind moving one bag for your gran
sit down and move the bags onto the floor yourself
stand for the whole journey because she said the seats are hers
complain to the train manager about her hogging seats
payload.explanation: A polite ask gives her the chance to do the right thing.

payload.snippet: Your friend pulls the emergency cord on the train as a joke because she wants to see what happens, but the fine is hundreds of pounds if caught.
options: tell the guard honestly when they come and apologise together
pretend it wasn't you when the guard comes round
blame another passenger you don't know for pulling it
swap seats with your friend so the guard asks her
payload.explanation: Honest apology usually beats hiding when the guard arrives.

payload.snippet: Your little brother is bored on the long train journey and starts kicking the seat in front, where a woman is trying to sleep and getting more annoyed.
options: swap seats with him and bring out the colouring book
tell him off loudly so the woman knows you tried
let him carry on because it's a six hour train ride
apologise to the woman but don't change anything yet
payload.explanation: Swapping seats and a colouring book actually stops the kicking.

payload.snippet: Your phone falls down the gap between the train and the platform at a quiet country station, and the next train is in two hours with no staff in sight.
options: press the emergency intercom on the platform for help
lie on the platform and try to reach down for it yourself
wait two hours and try to grab it before the next train
give up and tell mum the phone is lost forever
payload.explanation: Intercoms exist exactly for between-train-and-platform emergencies.

payload.snippet: The man in the seat opposite is loudly arguing on his phone in a way that's clearly upsetting your gran, and the carriage is packed so you can't easily move.
options: ask him politely to take the call to the vestibule
glare at him hard until he notices and stops talking
tell gran to put her headphones in to block him out
record his call on your phone to play back to him
payload.explanation: A polite ask works on most adults in a packed carriage.

payload.snippet: You're travelling alone for the first time and you suddenly realise you got on the wrong train at the previous stop, and you're heading away from your destination.
options: ask the conductor at the next stop how to get back
panic and get off at the very next stop on your own
phone home and cry while staying on the wrong train
stay on hoping the train will turn round eventually
payload.explanation: Conductors know every connection and will get you back.

payload.snippet: Your friend wants to record a TikTok dancing in the train aisle while the train is moving, and other passengers are squeezing past trying to reach the toilet.
options: suggest filming at the station after you both get off
film it anyway because the journey is the best part
film a shorter version so the passengers aren't blocked
stand watch so she gets warned when people are coming
payload.explanation: Station platforms have space and steady ground for dancing videos.

payload.snippet: Your train is delayed an hour and your friend who promised to pick you up at the station is sat in the car park with no phone signal at the other end.
options: find the station free wifi and message her over that
walk home from the station even though it's miles away
wait at the platform and hope she eventually leaves
ask a stranger to lend you their phone for free
payload.explanation: Station wifi reaches the car park and saves everyone waiting.

payload.snippet: You're queuing for the toilet on the train and a much older lady joins behind you looking really uncomfortable, fidgeting and clearly needing it more urgently than you.
options: offer her your place in the queue with a smile
pretend not to notice and use the toilet first yourself
ask everyone in front to let her skip the whole queue
stand aside and wait for everyone after her to go too
payload.explanation: Offering your place is the small kind thing on a long journey.

payload.snippet: Your seat reservation is on a train that's been cancelled and the next train is rammed, but your reserved seat number on the new train has another passenger sleeping in it.
options: show your reservation to the guard and let them sort it
wake the sleeping passenger and demand your seat back
stand for the whole journey because the train is rammed
take any free seat and complain online about it later
payload.explanation: Guards handle reservation clashes — that's literally their job.

payload.snippet: Your group of school friends are messing around on the platform and one of them is leaning over the edge to see how close the train comes, with the train one minute away.
options: pull her gently back and tell her how close the train is
tell her to lean further so it makes a better TikTok
tell the platform staff before the train arrives now
wait until the train comes and laugh about it later
payload.explanation: Pulling her back gently saves a TikTok from becoming a tragedy.

payload.snippet: Your gran left her handbag on the train when you got off, and inside is her glasses, her purse, and the only photo she has of grandad as a young man.
options: tell station staff right now and give them gran's details
wait until you get home and phone lost property tomorrow
buy gran a new bag with similar bits to replace it
blame gran for not paying enough attention to her bag
payload.explanation: Station staff radio ahead and often catch bags at the next stop.

payload.snippet: Your friend who has hayfever is sneezing constantly on the train and the woman across the aisle keeps making loud unkind comments about catching her germs.
options: calmly tell the woman it's hayfever and offer your friend tissues
argue loudly with the woman about being prejudiced about sneezing
swap seats so your friend is further from the woman
ignore it and pretend you can't hear the woman's comments
payload.explanation: Calm facts about hayfever shut down unkind comments without a fight.

payload.snippet: You see someone slip a phone out of the bag of a sleeping passenger sitting two rows ahead, and they're now putting the phone into their own pocket quietly.
options: press the call button discreetly and wait for the guard
shout 'thief' loudly across the whole train carriage
tackle the person yourself to get the phone back fast
wake the sleeping passenger and tell them what happened
payload.explanation: Call buttons get the guard there safely without confrontation.

payload.snippet: Your scout group is taking up six seats in priority seating and an elderly man with a stick has just got on at a stop with no other free seats left.
options: stand up and offer him a priority seat with the others
pretend not to see him and hope he asks someone else
leave only one priority seat free and keep the rest
ask the leader if you have to give up your seats
payload.explanation: Priority seats exist for exactly this man's situation right now.

payload.snippet: Your phone shows the train is replacing the rail line with a bus, but your gran isn't great with buses and the rail staff can't tell you exactly when it'll arrive.
options: ask staff to arrange assisted travel for gran on the bus
leave gran at the station and complete the journey alone
wait for any later train rather than using the bus
tell gran she'll have to manage the bus alone today
payload.explanation: Assisted travel makes the bus possible and gran feel safer.

payload.snippet: Your seat is by an open window and the wind is freezing the gran in the seat behind, but the man next to you says he's hot and wants the window open further.
options: suggest closing it slightly and ask the guard about temperature
close the window and let the man complain to the guard
leave it open because grandma will warm up eventually
tell gran to swap seats with you for the rest of the journey
payload.explanation: A small compromise plus guard input solves both temperatures.

payload.snippet: You're alone on a quiet late train and a passenger starts asking you personal questions and which station you're getting off at, making you really uncomfortable.
options: move to the carriage with the guard and stay there
answer the questions politely so they leave you alone
lie about your station so they get off at the wrong place
shout at them loudly so other passengers hear you
payload.explanation: The guard's carriage has staff and CCTV and stops the questions.
